answer.policy_title: Surgery of the Ankle (UnitedHealthcare Commercial and Individual Exchange Medical Policy / UnitedHealthcare Oxford Clinical Policy)
criteria_quotes: Surgery of the ankle is proven and medically necessary in certain circumstances. For medical necessity clinical coverage criteria, refer to the InterQual® CP: Procedures: ... Total Joint Replacement (TJR), Ankle
answer.submission_route: By Mail: Oxford Health Plans, Attn: Clinical Appeals, PO Box 29139, Hot Springs, AR 71903. By Phone: Contact Oxford/UnitedHealthcare Member Services at 1-800-444-6222 or 1-800-666-1353. Online: Submit an appeal/grievance form online through the member portal at myuhc.com or via uhc.com.
answer.how_to_obtain_criteria: Because UnitedHealthcare and Oxford utilize proprietary InterQual® criteria (licensed from Optum) for total ankle replacement reviews, the specific medical-necessity checklists are not printed directly in the public policy document. Under the Affordable Care Act (ACA), the patient has a legal right to receive a copy of the specific clinical review criteria used to deny their claim, free of charge. The patient can obtain these criteria by calling Member Services at the number on the back of their ID card (or 1-800-444-6222) and requesting the 'InterQual CP: Procedures: Total Joint Replacement (TJR), Ankle' criteria applied to their case. Alternatively, providers and members can view a read-only version of the InterQual criteria on UHCprovider.com under 'Policies > Clinical Guidelines > InterQual Clinical Criteria' after logging in with a One Healthcare ID.
answer.notes: The denial letter references a commercial/ACA Oxford plan in New Jersey. UnitedHealthcare Oxford Clinical Policies align directly with the UnitedHealthcare Commercial Medical Policies. Both the UHC Commercial policy 'Surgery of the Ankle' (Policy 2026T0622O) and the Oxford Clinical Policy 'Surgery of the Ankle' utilize identical guidelines and defer to the third-party InterQual® clinical criteria for CPT code 27702 (Arthroplasty, ankle; with implant).

Date of notice: 2026-08-16
Member: Cameron Carter
Member ID: W300143742
Plan: UnitedHealthcare / Oxford (Commercial/ACA), state of New Jersey

Dear Cameron,

We reviewed the prior authorization request submitted by your provider for the following service:

    Requested service: Total ankle replacement
    Procedure code (CPT): 27702

After review, this request is DENIED. Reason for determination: the requested procedure does not meet the plan's criteria for medical necessity.

This determination was made under the plan's applicable medical policy and clinical review criteria. You have the right to appeal this decision. Your appeal must be received within 180 days of the date of this notice (by 2027-02-12).

Reference number: POC-3469ABE4FC-29435

In osteoarthritis, the cartilage in the joint gradually wears away. As the cartilage wears away, it becomes frayed and rough, and the protective space between the bones decreases. This can result in bone rubbing on bone and produce painful osteophytes (bone spurs). Posttraumatic arthritis can develop after an injury to the foot or ankle, and dislocations and fractures are the most common injuries that lead to posttraumatic arthritis. Like osteoarthritis, posttraumatic arthritis causes the cartilage between the joints to wear away and can develop many years after the initial injury. Future studies, including randomized controlled trials with comparison groups, are needed, along with long-term results. Wen et al. (2025) conducted a PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses)– registered systematic review under PROSPERO, evaluating the long-term clinical efficacy and safety of surgical treatments of osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLTs), with a minimum 5-year follow-up. Studies included adults aged over 18 years from prospective or retrospective cohort, case-control, or case series studies with more than five individuals. There were 43 studies, with 2,721 individuals (62.2% male) aged 23.9 to 47.7 years and who had defect sizes of 0.9 to 29.1 cm2 included in the review, which evaluated a total of 13 joint-preservation techniques and included follow- up durations of 5 to 24.1 years. The outcomes assessed included patient-reported outcomes, return to activity, complications, and failures. All studies that were included were non–randomized controlled trials and level IV evidence. The authors concluded that the most common technique used was bone marrow stimulator (BMS), primarily for smaller lesions, and that it produced comparable survival rates compared with all other techniques. Additionally, they concluded that treatments should be personalized and evidence based and should consider lesion characteristics and patient factors. Limitations include the high heterogeneity across studies due to wide lesion size ranges and characteristics of the lesion. Additionally, the majority of studies were noncomparative in design and level IV evidence, which limits the strength of the findings and prevents meta-analysis of pooled data; several studies that were included had small sample sizes; objective measures used for patient-reported outcomes were lacking; concomitant or previous procedures were not controlled for; and baseline demographics were not often stratified into subgroups, which limited comparability and the conduction of a meta-analysis. Correia Cardoso et al. (2024) conducted a systematic review that evaluated the operative treatment of nonprimary OLTs. The review included 50 studies, which involved 806 ankles of 794 individuals. The majority of the studies were retrospective in design, and only 14% included a comparison group. The Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine was used and showed that 86% of the studies were classified as level 4 evidence. All studies exhibited a high risk of bias in at least one domain, with 64% demonstrating a high risk across at least four domains. Cartilage substitution was the most common treatment, including 30% osteochondral autograft and 11% osteochondral allograft. Cartilage regeneration, comprising 37%, included 9% autologous chondrocyte implantation (ACI), 8% matrix-assisted autologous chondrocyte transplant, 2% bone marrow–derived cell transplant, and 17% autologous matrix-induced chondrogenesis (AMIC). Rescue procedures/HemiCAP and cartilage repair/BMS accounted for 14% and 9%, respectively. The AOFAS score was reported in 54% of the studies, and the mean improvement ranged from 13 to 57.8, with osteochondral autograft showing the most and least pronounced mean change. The pre- to postoperative meta-analysis revealed significant improvements across all treatments (p < 0.05), except for osteochondral allograft, which showed no significant improvement. The highest success rates were seen with ACI and osteochondral autograft, whereas HemiCAP had the lowest. The visual analog scale/numeric rating scale for pain score was reported in 48% of studies and showed mean improvements that ranged from 1.5 to 8, with osteochondral autograft displaying the most pronounced mean change and HemiCAP showing the lowest. The pre- to postoperative meta-analysis revealed significant improvements across most treatments (p < 0.05), with ACI demonstrating a large effect size, while osteochondral allograft and HemiCAP showed no significant improvements. The highest success rates were seen with ACI and osteochondral autograft, while HemiCAP had the lowest. The postoperative subjective satisfaction was reported in 46% of the studies, with a high rate of success across all operative treatments; AMIC and HemiCAP had the lowest rates. HemiCAP had the highest incidence of postoperative complications, and clinical failures were more frequent with AMIC (27%), osteochondral autograft (22%), osteochondral allograft (19%), and HemiCAP (28%). While ACI and osteochondral autograft showed improvements and higher success rates than HemiCAP and osteochondral allograft, the authors noted that despite the promising potential, the high risk of bias across the included studies warrants a cautious interpretation of these results. Limitations of the study include the high risk of selection and detection bias; retrospective nature; predominance of case series; variability in study designs and outcome measures; lack of comparison groups; use of nonvalidated outcome measures; and insufficient reporting of demographic variations and lesion characteristics.
